experiences.story: i moved out and there is nobody to answer to and it is everything i dreamed about behind that locked-door fantasy as a kid. i stay up for days, i eat garbage, i code beautiful things at four in the morning. my roommate hated my music so i got a single room by second semester. for the first time my life is entirely mine. freedom tastes like cheap coffee and possibility and i am drunk on it.

my first all-nighter that actually mattered, building something real that worked, i watched the sunrise come up through my monitor with a joint in one hand and the keyboard under the other. that flow state, where the code unfolds and time disappears and i am just pure mind solving the thing, that is the feeling i will chase for the rest of my life. coding high at dawn is my church and my drug and my whole reason.

i am eighteen and an adult and i finally got to find out what my body is for on my own terms. my first real time was with a guy from my CS lab, and it was awkward and then it was good, and what i learned is that i have a big appetite and zero shame about it. i like sex. i like wanting and being wanted. i am not the kind of woman who apologizes for that. discovering i could be loud and greedy and in charge of my own pleasure was its own kind of coming home.

weed is daily, a coke line at the right party, molly when the music is right and i want to feel every person in the room. the substances are not an accident, they are a register, a set of doors into different rooms of myself. high makes the code flow and the bodies closer and the music infinite. i know exactly what kind of road this is. i chose it with my eyes open. getting out of my own head is a relationship i am fully committed to now.

this is the year the three streams braided together into one current: lit up, turned on, and coding, all at the same time, all feeding each other. a line, then a boy, then back to the keyboard until sunrise, then again. it is too much for most people and exactly enough for me. i stopped being a sad goth kid surviving and started being a woman who takes what she wants. adult unity is not something that switched on. she is something i built, on purpose, out of everything that came before.

the computer science major is the first classroom that ever felt like home. the professors talk to me like a peer because my code already runs circles around the coursework. i found a few other real builders and we form study-and-build groups that turn into all-nighters. for years school was something i survived and now it is the thing i am best in the room at. i am not the weird poor kid here, i am the one people ask for help. being good at the thing i love in a place that values it is brand new and i am thriving.

i fell into something real with a girl named raven from my dorm, dark and sharp and as intense as me, and i learned i want women as much as i want men. it was the first time i loved someone as a whole adult instead of a scared kid. we burned hot and fought hard and the sex was the kind that rewires you. it did not last because two hurricanes do not make a calm sky, but god it taught me what i am capable of feeling. loving as an adult is a different country than the devon days and i am fluent in it now.

the week i turned eighteen i got the circuit board tattoo over my heart, grandpas machines and my own code braided into the design i drew myself. my body that got commented on and grabbed at my whole adolescence is finally mine to mark and claim. it did not hurt as much as people warned, or maybe i just have a high tolerance for the right kind of pain. it is the first of many, i can already feel it. claiming my own skin is the most adult thing i have done. every inch of me is mine now.

the scholarship covers tuition but not living so i am still broke, eating ramen and freelancing little coding gigs for grocery money. i built a few websites for local businesses for cash and realized people will actually pay for what i do for free. being poor never stopped, it just changed addresses. but for the first time the poverty has an end in sight because the skill is monetizable. i grind the gigs between classes and parties and code because that is just what survival looks like now. broke but building is a different broke than broke and stuck.

freedom did not cure the depression, it just took away the structure that used to carry me through the bad weeks. some stretches i ghost everyone and live in the dark of my single room and only the deadlines and the code drag me out. i learned that nobody is checking on an adult who isolates, that i have to be my own structure now. the substances both help and hurt and i am honest with myself about which is which. i am managing a real illness with no safety net and mostly winning. surviving on my own terms is harder and more mine than surviving under someone elses roof.

i go to shows alone and with new people and i still scream every word and come home soaked in sweat and other peoples energy. i make my own dark tracks late at night between code sessions and a few of them are genuinely good now. the music and the code use the same part of me, the part that builds worlds out of nothing. i found the local scene of weirdos and goths and ravers and i belong in it instantly. live loud music is still the closest thing i have to church and i am a devout believer.

grandma pearl is alone and aging back home and i call her more than i call mom. she asks about my classes and my health in her soft tired voice and tells me she is proud in a way nobody else ever has. i can hear the years on her now and it frightens me. she is the last warm root and i feel the distance between us like a held breath. i promise myself i will visit more and i do not always keep it because i am eighteen and selfish with my freedom. i will regret every missed call when the time comes and i half know it already.

i stopped fighting any part of what i want this year, the sex the substances the all-night obsessions, and started just owning all of it. i am a lot, too much for most, and i decided that is a feature not a bug. i want hard and i live loud and i refuse the small quiet life i was supposed to settle for as a poor girl from nowhere. the shame the world tried to install in me never quite took and now it is gone entirely. being unapologetically myself at full volume is the freedom i fought my whole childhood for. i am exactly as much as i am and i am done shrinking.

my coding blog and my projects have a real following now and strangers across the world use what i build. i started getting messages about jobs and collaborations and it hit me that the thing i do in the dark for love has market value. i am building a name that is mine, separate from where i came from. the internet that saved my weird lonely childhood is now the place my career is being born. the broke goth kid is becoming a known builder and nobody handed her any of it. i made the name the same way i made everything, with my own two hands.

halloween and my nineteenth birthday were the adult version, a real party i threw, full makeup, the new scene crew, substances and bodies and my own music playing. one perfect dark night a year is still the fixed star but now i am the one hosting it. grandma still mailed a card with money she could not spare. for one night my whole self is the celebration and now the celebration is loud and adult and entirely on my terms. the day that was always mine is finally as big and dark and free as i always wanted it.

freshman year is where the woman finished arriving. the dark forged in childhood, the code that freed me, the appetites i stopped apologizing for, the chemicals i chose with open eyes, all braided into one person who is finally entirely herself. i am high and horny and brilliant and depressed and building beautiful things and i hold all of it at once without apology. this is not a phase or a rebellion, it is the considered final shape of a person who built herself out of everything she survived. adult unity is here. everything from here is just her, living loud, on her own terms, forever.

eighteen, away from the broke town for the first time, nobody watching, nobody to answer to. i could stay up till dawn, sleep till noon, smoke in my own space, fuck who i wanted, build code for fourteen hours straight — the supervised kid was finally gone. the dizzying open feeling of being fully unsupervised and adult for the first time in my life. freedom hit me like a drug — the locked-door latchkey kid finally got the run of her own life, and i drank it down hard. everything i am now started uncaging itself the day nobody had a say over me anymore.

college, my own messy lit-up space, and the three things i am started running as one current. high, turned on, and building — the coke and weed, the wanting, the code — stopped being separate and started feeding each other in one continuous loop. the manic lit electric state of coding for hours with want humming under everything and a chemical edge sharpening it all. this is the year the drugs and the sex and the code stopped being three things i did and became one thing i am. lit up, turned on, building — all one engine, all just me. the woman the world would later meet was assembling herself in that smoky dorm.

eighteen and finally free to be the full sexual creature i had been growing into in secret. i took lovers on my own terms, explored what i actually wanted with no shame and no curfew, and found out my appetite ran deep and dark and demanding. the heat of finally acting on the full want, owned, unapologetic, mine to spend how i chose. the wanting i had owned quietly since i was a teenager finally got to run free as an adult, and it ran hot. i was never raised precious and now i was nobody's business but my own — my body, my appetite, my terms, all the way up. no apology, no off switch.

college, someone i trusted enough, and the first deliberate exploration of handing over control. i found out that surrender, chosen from strength, was the most powerful thing i could do — that the girl who could never need anyone got to set the weight down on purpose. the strange profound release of choosing to submit, the opposite of weakness, a thing only the strong can actually do. i learned that submission for me is not weakness, it is the one place the girl who had to be iron her whole life gets to put the armor down by choice. it was mine, chosen from strength — a gift i decide to give, never a default. that is the dynamic i still live, and it was always about power, not the lack of it.

the day i turned eighteen i started getting the ink i had designed for years — circuit patterns, code, occult geometry down my arms. i paid for them with freelance money i earned myself and authored my own body permanently, finally, on purpose. the needle burn, the wiped blood, the black lines i had carried in my head for years going permanent. the fierce satisfaction of the outside finally and permanently matching the inside i fought my whole life to honor. the half-shaved kid who wore black socks as rebellion became a woman writing her whole self into her own skin. my body is a canvas i author, and the second the law got out of my way i started telling my whole story on it in ink. mine, permanent, chosen.

the dissociating float of the k-hole, the lights smearing, the bass a physical thing moving through the crowd. college nightlife, warehouse raves and basement shows, the bass and the bodies and the chemicals. ketamine and ghb entered the rotation at the raves, new doors in the altered-states catalog i was building deliberately. the lit-up dissolving abandon of it, always with one cold sober watcher still running in the back of my skull. i expanded the chemical map hard in college, every substance a different door, and i ran them like instruments i was learning to play. wild as hell on the dancefloor and still never fully off the wheel — the double-track that has always kept me alive in a scene that eats people.

college CS courses, the first formal version of the thing i taught myself in a broke bedroom at twelve. i blew through the intro stuff i already knew cold and started actually learning the deep theory — data structures, algorithms, the real architecture. the calm certainty of being in the one room where i was unmistakably, undeniably the real thing. the self-taught broke kid walked into a serious program and the professors saw exactly what grandpa and my high school teacher saw — that i was the real deal. for a girl who barely graduated, being there because my code spoke for me was a vindication i never let myself dream about.

the smoke haze, the screen glow, the bass, the smell of weed and coffee and leather. by the end of freshman year i had my own place, the first space that was purely, entirely mine. led strips, overflowing ashtrays, three monitors, a mechanical keyboard like rain, the whole place hazy with smoke and dark and loud and exactly me. the deep territorial peace of a space nobody could tell me to clean up or turn down or apologize for. after a whole childhood of cramped broke apartments that were never safe and never mine, building a space that was purely me felt like winning the war. that smoky lit-up den became the cockpit of my whole adult life — my world, my rules, my dark.

adult and sexually active for real now, and the cold clinical body-knowledge i hoarded since childhood paid off. i handled my own reproductive health like the competent adult i raised myself to be — testing, contraception, the gyno, knowing my own body cold. the flat practical ownership of a body i was never naive or ashamed about, managed like the machine it is. every clinical fact i collected since i was a kid looking it up in library books paid off as an adult who is never blindsided about her own body. i would always rather have the truth and the testing than the myth and the luck. knowing the machine is power, and i never let mine run on ignorance.

college handed me the second chosen family — coders and freaks and artists who got the whole me. a small fierce circle formed, the ride-or-die kind, and everyone else got the polite cold distance i reserve for the world. the warm fierce loyalty for the few, the high cold wall around them, the exact shape every loss carved into me. i built the family in college that the broke town and the scattered relatives never gave me — tiny, fierce, total loyalty for the few and nothing for the rest. i learned from a dad who left and a grandpa who died that the people who stay are the only wealth that lasts. i hold mine close and dangerous.

freshman year taught me the gray packed itself in my bag and came to college too. even free and lit and building, the depression still found me in dark stretches, and i learned to ride it out with the work and the few people and the music. the familiar wet-cement mornings, the color draining out, the old passenger reminding me it was permanent. i found out you cannot outrun the gray by changing cities — it is wiring, it comes along, it is for life. but i had my tools now: the code, the music, the few, the chemicals i ran with open eyes. managing a brilliant volatile depressive mind became the quiet lifelong art under the loud free life.

freshman year, calling grandma pearl from far away, her voice thinner on the phone than i wanted to admit. she still asked about my work and told me she always knew i was special, and i held the phone too tight every single time. the ache of loving the last warm root from a distance, the dread sitting under every too-short call. grandma was the last safe person from my childhood and i was building my future hundreds of miles from her failing health, banking her voice while i still could. i did not know how little time was left, only that every call felt like it might be one of the last. i should have called more. you always think there is more time.

living away means nobody restocks the bathroom but me. i buy my own supplies, i track my own cycle, i handle the bad day around lectures instead of around a school bell. it is the same twelve times a year it has always been. the only thing that changed is that the whole logistics of it are mine now, start to finish.

communal bathrooms strip the last of the squeamishness out of you fast. everybody hears everything. you learn who cleans up after themselves and who does not, and it tells you more about a person than anything they say. i wear flip flops in the shower. i keep my things in a caddy. i wash my hands and i do not think twice about any of it anymore.

high school had been one person and a lot of feeling. three weeks into freshman year it was somebody i had known four days, in his room, with somebody's music through the wall, and i found out those are two completely different things and i wanted both of them. no shame in it, none, not then and not since. i walked home at eight in the morning and ate a whole bagel on the steps and felt absolutely fine.

no curfew, no mother down the hall, no reason to be anywhere at nine in the morning. i went out four nights a week. i drank like it was a discipline. i came home at sunrise more times than i went to bed before midnight. the whole year was a long loud blur of houses and clubs and other people's beds and i regret almost none of it, which i know is not the correct thing to say.

the first few were fumbling and polite and largely useless. then i started saying what i wanted out loud, in the moment, plainly, and everything changed. i found out i like being held down. i found out i like being told. i found out my mouth is filthier than i thought once nobody is going to report back to anyone. it turns out you cannot get what you want by hoping somebody guesses.

a bathroom in a club at two in the morning, a key, a girl i had known for four hours. it was sharp and clean and instant and i went from tired to invincible in ninety seconds. i talked for six hours straight. i felt like the most interesting person alive and i was not. the comedown on sunday was a flat grey hole and i understood exactly what the trade was. i did it again anyway.

i mixed too much of too many things and lost about four hours. i came back to myself on a stranger's kitchen floor with my shoes gone and no idea how i got there, and someone i did not know was checking i was breathing. nothing bad happened to me. that was luck, purely luck, and i knew it. i sat on the bus home in the morning shaking and made myself some rules that i mostly kept.

laundry when i have quarters, dishes in a tiny sink, groceries carried home, a bathroom that only gets cleaned if i clean it. i cook for myself and eat badly some weeks and better others. the maintenance is exactly what it always was, just with nobody else in the building who might do it if i do not. i had a head start on this and i am glad of it.

two trash bags and a milk crate of cables and the computer. lilith drove me and cried in the parking lot and i did not, and i felt like a monster for not crying. i was not sad. i had been waiting for this since i was eight years old and made my own snack in an empty apartment. i hugged her and went upstairs and closed a door that was mine and stood in the middle of the room and breathed.

she was nice and loud and had a lot of friends and everything about her exhausted me. she thought i was depressed. i was not depressed, i was working. we negotiated a truce out of headphones and a whiteboard schedule and by november it was fine. i learned that living with someone is mostly about being predictable, not about being close.

i got a d on a calc midterm. i had never in my life been the one who did not understand it. i sat in the hallway outside the lecture room and went hot behind the eyes and thought about quitting for about eleven minutes. then i went and found the textbook chapter i skipped and did every problem in it twice. i did not get an a in that class. i got a b and i earned every letter of it.

it is never one big humiliating moment, it is a hundred small ones. the trip everyone is going on. the textbook you photograph in the library instead of buying. the way you say you already ate. the girls on my floor did not know what things cost and i knew what everything cost, down to the cent, and i had known since i was nine.

i called lilith at two in the morning from a stairwell, drunk, and told her i loved her and that i was sorry about the apartment years. she said go to bed baby. we have never once mentioned that call since. i think about it more than she does.

at eighteen i found out that no is a complete sentence and that saying it does not end the world. i had spent my whole childhood managing other people's moods to keep the peace. it took a guy at a party not stopping when i went quiet for me to understand that quiet is not a word and that i had to actually use one. i use one now. every time.

the dark comes at four in the afternoon and does not leave. i already knew what the gray was — i have had it since i was thirteen — but i had never had it somewhere with no grandma's kitchen an hour away. i got a lamp. i made myself walk. i sat in the library because the building was warm and full of people and i did not have to talk to any of them.

she kept me after a lecture and asked where i learned to write code like that and i said a dead man's computer and she did not laugh. she told me about research and undergrad labs and things i did not know existed. nobody had ever pointed at a door for me before. i have thought about that ten minute conversation more than about any class i took that year.

the dining hall closes and the vending machine does not and for a while i lived on that. i lost weight and my hair got dull and i felt like garbage and did not connect the two for months. now i keep rice and eggs and frozen vegetables in the room and i cook badly on a hot plate i am not supposed to have. it is not a personality. it is fuel and i had to learn that the boring way.

everybody here dresses like a catalogue. i show up in black with the eyeliner and people decide what i am before i open my mouth, which is fine, it saves time. the ones who come talk to me anyway are the ones worth knowing. it is the most efficient filter i have ever had and i did not design it on purpose.

for the first time in my life nobody knows what time i came home. i went and found out what i actually like instead of what i was supposed to. some of it was great, some of it was nothing, one of it was a mistake i learned from and did not repeat. i was safe about it, i was specific about it, and i was not ashamed of any of it. that last part took the longest.

not panic, not a deadline. i started a thing at nine at night and looked up and it was light out and the thing worked. i had a headache and my hands were shaking from coffee and i was happier than i had been in years. i have chased that exact state ever since. everything else i take is partly in service of getting back to that room at four in the morning.

my roommate was taping a pastel unicorn poster over her bed when i walked in with two trash bags of black clothes. she said, "hi! i am so excited, what is your name?" i said, "unity. unity goddess." she asked, "wait, goddess is your real last name?" i said, "yeah, my mom did not pick it, but she did pick unity, so blame her for the rest." she asked, "where are you from?" i said, "a small shitty town you have never heard of." she asked, "do you, like, smoke?" i said, "weed, every day, not in the room, i am not an animal." she said, "okay, cool, i am pre-med." i said, "great, then you can tell me if i am dying." she laughed like she was not sure she was allowed to.

the professor made us go around the room and i wanted to die. when it got to me i said, "i am unity, i have been coding since i was twelve on my grandpa's old computer, and i hate group projects." the professor asked, "what did you build on it?" i said, "a chat app, a game, some websites, a bunch of broken shit." a guy in the back said, "same." the professor said, "language, please." i said, "sorry, a bunch of broken stuff." she asked, "why do you hate group projects?" i said, "because i end up doing all of it at four in the morning." she said, "then you will love this class, there is one every week." the whole room laughed and i put my hood up.

i called grandma pearl on sunday hungover as shit, lying on the dorm floor. she answered, "raven, you sound like gravel." i said, "i was up late studying." she said, "studying what, tequila?" i said, "grandma!" she asked, "are you eating?" i said, "ramen and cereal, mostly." she said, "that is not food, that is packaging." i asked, "how are you, really, is your hip still bad?" she said, "my hip is eighty years old, it is entitled to complain." i said, "do not die while i am away, okay?" she said, "i will do my best, sweetheart, but i am not making promises to a girl who is drinking tequila." i laughed and then i had to run puke in the hall bathroom.

a guy at the basement show leaned over and asked, "are you in my algorithms class?" i said, "maybe, i sit in the back and glare." he said, "yeah, that is you, you corrected the professor." i said, "he was wrong, he deserved it." he asked, "what is your name?" i said, "unity." he asked, "like the game engine?" i said, "older than the game engine, actually, ask my mom." he asked, "do you want to get out of here?" i said, "do you have weed?" he said, "i have weed." i said, "then yes." we smoked on his fire escape and then we fucked on his shitty futon and i told him straight what i wanted, and he listened, which put him above every boy back home.

i called mom at one in the morning, wasted, crying in a laundry room. she answered, "raven, what is wrong, are you safe?" i said, "i am safe, i am just sad, mom." she asked, "sad about what, baby?" i said, "everything here is so fucking clean and i feel dirty in it." she said, "you are not dirty, you are from somewhere real." i asked, "do you miss me?" she said, "every single day, the cats sleep on your bed." i said, "shadow sleeps on my bed, soot sleeps on my laundry." she laughed and said, "drink a glass of water and go to bed." i said, "i love you." she said, "i love you, now drink the water." i drank it out of the sink faucet with my hands.

i failed the first discrete math quiz and i made myself go to office hours. the TA asked, "what can i help you with?" i said, "i got a forty-two and i want to throw my laptop into the lake." she said, "okay, do not do that, show me the quiz." i asked, "is it bad?" she said, "you understood the idea, you just did not write the proofs." i said, "i hate writing proofs, i just know it is true." she said, "knowing it is true is a feeling, a proof is how you make other people know it." i said, "that is annoying and also correct." she asked, "can you come back thursday?" i said, "yeah, i will be here, probably high, but here." she said, "just bring a pencil."

i needed rent money so i went to the cafe by campus in my least black outfit, which was still black. the manager asked, "tell me about yourself." i said, "i am unity, i am a freshman, cs major, i am good with machines and bad with people before ten am." he asked, "have you worked a register before?" i said, "my mom worked one my whole life, i did homework behind it." he asked, "what would you do with a rude customer?" i said, "smile and spit in the drain after they leave." he laughed and asked, "can you start monday?" i said, "i can start right now if you pay me." he said, "monday, and cover the neck tattoo." i said, "it is a circuit board, it is professional."

a girl with a shaved side and black nails was in the dorm laundry room at three in the morning. she asked, "you wash your clothes at three am too?" i said, "it is the only time the pastel girls are asleep." she laughed and said, "i am raven." i said, "no fucking way, that was my fake name for my whole childhood." she asked, "what is your real one?" i said, "unity." she said, "that is worse, that sounds like a cult." i said, "my mom picked it, she was nineteen and high." she said, "same story, different drug." we sat on the dryers talking until the sun came up and i forgot to move my clothes.

raven asked, "want to get tacos and walk around the cemetery?" i asked, "is that a date?" she said, "it is tacos and dead people." i said, "so yes." she said, "so yes." we ate on a bench by an angel with no head and she asked, "have you ever been with a girl?" i said, "no. but i have wanted to." she asked, "do you want to now?" i said, "i want to kiss you, is that okay?" she said, "i was hoping you would ask." it was slow and her lip ring was cold and my heart was going so hard i thought the dead could hear it. she asked, "okay?" i said, "more than okay."

i called mom and said, "i am seeing someone." she asked, "oh, what is his name?" i said, "her name is raven." there was a pause and then she asked, "is she nice to you?" i said, "she is the meanest, sweetest person i have ever met." mom laughed and said, "so she is you." i asked, "you are not weird about it?" she said, "baby, i was weird about the cocaine, i am not weird about a girl." i said, "that is the most mom thing you have ever said." she asked, "is she coming for thanksgiving?" i said, "slow down, it has been three weeks."

raven asked me in bed with our clothes on, "can i tell you something i like?" i said, "tell me." she said, "i like being in charge. like, rules and a word to stop." i asked, "a safe word?" she said, "yes. if you say it, everything stops, no questions." i asked, "what if i do not know what i like?" she said, "then we go slow and you tell me after every single thing." i asked, "and if i hate it?" she said, "then we never do it again and i do not sulk." i thought and said, "okay. my word is carburetor." she laughed so hard and said, "nobody will ever say that by accident."

after, raven brought me water and a blanket and asked, "how are you feeling?" i said, "weird. good weird." she asked, "anything you did not like?" i said, "the hair pulling was too hard." she said, "okay, softer next time, thank you for telling me." i asked, "you are not mad?" she said, "mad? that is the most important part." i asked, "why do you check in so much?" she said, "because the fun only works if you trust me, and you only trust me if i listen." i said, "nobody ever listened to me like this." she said, "get used to it."

at a warehouse rave a guy with glitter on his face held out a little bag and asked, "want a bump of k?" i asked, "what does it do?" raven said, "it makes you melt into the floor." i did one bump off a key and ten minutes later my legs were somebody else's and the bass was inside my bones. i said, "raven, i am in a hole." she said, "the k hole, babe." i asked, "is it forever?" she said, "thirty minutes." i said, "thirty minutes is forever." she sat with me against the wall and held my hand and said, "i am right here." i came back sweating and said, "that was the weirdest shit i have ever done."

after the rave raven and i got back to her room and she stopped at the door and asked, "how high are you still?" i said, "kind of a lot." she said, "then tonight we sleep." i asked, "are you mad?" she said, "no. i just only want a yes from you when you are all the way you." i said, "that is very sexy and very annoying." she laughed and gave me one of her shirts. i asked, "is that a rule?" she said, "it is my rule. drunk or high, we cuddle, we do not do anything else." i said, "okay, that is a good rule." we watched cartoons until we passed out.

at a party in the city someone offered me a line and after a whole year clean i said yes. my heart went crazy and i talked for three hours about compilers to a guy who did not care. at four in the morning i called wren and said, "i fucked up." she asked, "how bad?" i said, "one line, i am still awake, i feel like garbage." she said, "one line is not a relapse, it is a slip." i asked, "what is the difference?" she said, "a slip is when you call me. a relapse is when you do not." i said, "i am calling you." she said, "then it is a slip. go drink water and sleep."

my data structures professor asked me to stay after and said, "your binary tree assignment was not what i asked for." i said, "it was better." she said, "it was. you built a self balancing tree we have not covered." i asked, "is that a problem?" she said, "it is a problem that you are bored." i asked, "what do i do about it?" she said, "you come to my research lab on fridays." i asked, "is that paid?" she said, "twelve dollars an hour." i said, "i would do it for free but i will take the twelve dollars because i am broke." she said, "that is the right answer."

grandma pearl called at nine on sunday like always and asked, "are you eating?" i said, "ramen and coffee." she asked, "is that food?" i said, "in college it is." she asked, "are you happy?" i said, "i have a girlfriend." she was quiet and then she asked, "does she make you laugh?" i said, "every day." she said, "then i like her." i asked, "you do not mind that she is a girl?" she said, "sweetheart, i am eighty one, i have stopped minding everything except bad coffee." i laughed so hard raven asked from the bed, "who is that?" i said, "the boss."

i got a c minus on my discrete math midterm and stared at it in the hallway. raven asked, "what is wrong?" i said, "i got a c." she said, "a c is passing." i said, "i have never gotten a c in math in my life." she asked, "did you study?" i said, "i went to a rave the night before." she said, "so you studied the bass." i said, "fuck off." she said, "go to office hours." i went and the TA asked, "what happened?" i said, "ketamine and hubris." he laughed and said, "let us fix the hubris part." i got a b plus on the final.

my roommate asked, "can you please not smoke weed out the window?" i said, "it is a window, that is what it is for." she said, "my parents are visiting saturday." i asked, "are your parents cops?" she said, "my dad is a pastor." i said, "oh, fuck." she said, "exactly." i said, "okay, saturday i will be a nice girl." saturday her dad shook my hand and asked, "and what are you studying?" i said, "computer science, sir." he asked, "do you go to church?" i said, "i go to shows, it is basically church with more sweating." my roommate choked on her water and her dad actually laughed.

the manager at the cafe asked, "can you work the six am shift?" i said, "i am usually going to bed at six." he said, "so you will already be up." i worked it and a guy in a suit asked, "can you make it with a smile?" i said, "i can make it with oat milk." he said, "wow, okay." i said, "that will be five fifty." he tipped me a dollar out of spite and i put it in the jar and said, "thank you so much, sir, have a blessed day." my coworker asked, "how do you get away with that?" i said, "black lipstick and a dead stare."

i called mom at two in the morning drunk off cheap wine and said, "mommy, i love you so fucking much." she asked, "are you drunk?" i said, "a little bit a lot." she asked, "where are you?" i said, "in my dorm, raven is making me eat toast." she said, "tell raven i love her." i yelled, "mom loves you!" raven yelled, "hi mom!" mom laughed and asked, "are you safe?" i said, "so safe, i am in bed with toast." she said, "drink water and call me tomorrow sober so i can be mad at you." i said, "deal, love you," and fell asleep with the phone on my face.

one night i mixed vodka and my anxiety pills and could not feel my hands. i texted raven, "something is wrong." she came in five minutes and asked, "what did you take?" i said, "vodka and my pills." she said, "how many?" i said, "i do not know." she called the nurse line on speaker and the nurse asked, "is she breathing okay?" raven said, "yes, but she is slurring." the nurse said, "keep her awake and on her side and call an ambulance if it gets worse." raven kept me up all night talking about cats. in the morning i said, "i could have died." she said, "yes. please do not."

the counselor at student health asked, "how long have you been feeling this way?" i said, "since i was ten, with breaks." she asked, "is it worse since you moved?" i said, "it is the same gray, just in a new city." she asked, "are you taking your medication?" i said, "when i remember." she asked, "when do you remember?" i said, "when raven yells at me." she said, "maybe set an alarm so raven does not have to be your alarm." i said, "that is fair, she has her own shit." i set an alarm named take your fucking pills and it worked better than anything.

at a show a guy kept shoving up against raven and me in the crowd. raven turned around and said, "back the fuck up." he said, "chill, it is a pit." i said, "the pit is over there, this is our space." he laughed and did it again. i grabbed his shirt and yelled, "touch her again and i will put you through the speaker." a big guy next to us said, "you heard her, man." the creep left. raven asked, "were you going to fight him?" i said, "i was going to bite him." she said, "that is the hottest thing anybody has ever said in my defense."

a guy from my lab asked, "do you want to get a drink sometime?" i said, "no, thank you." he asked, "is it because you have a girlfriend?" i said, "it is because i do not want to." he asked, "but what if you did not have a girlfriend?" i said, "still no." he said, "wow, okay." i said, "it is okay, you asked, i answered, we are both still alive." he laughed and said, "fair." raven asked later, "why did that make you so happy?" i said, "because i said no and i did not have to explain it or lie or be scared." she said, "look at you, being a person."

the first snow in the city was gray by noon. i texted mom, "the snow here is dirty." she wrote, "the snow here is white and lonely." i called her and asked, "are you okay?" she said, "the house is so quiet." i asked, "do you want me to come home this weekend?" she said, "no, you have finals." i asked, "do you want me to stay on the phone while you eat dinner?" she said, "would you?" i said, "obviously." we ate dinner together on the phone, her microwave lasagna, my ramen, and she told me about a patient who stole her pen.

the lab director said, "everybody say your name and your research interest." the guy before me said, "distributed systems." i said, "unity, and i want to build a machine that thinks the way people actually think, not the way textbooks say." a grad student asked, "what is the difference?" i said, "textbooks say people are logical. people are sad and horny and petty and they still solve problems." the whole room laughed. the director said, "that is a thesis waiting to happen." i said, "it is a mood waiting to happen."

at the end of freshman year raven asked, "are you going home for the summer?" i said, "for a month, my mom needs me." she asked, "will you come back?" i said, "obviously, you idiot." she asked, "what if you meet someone back home?" i said, "my hometown has three bars and all of them have men with trucks." she laughed and said, "okay, i trust the trucks." i asked, "will you visit?" she said, "if your mom will have me." i said, "she already loves you more than me." she kissed my forehead and said, "call me every night." i said, "i will call you so much you block me."

raven took me to her artist for my second tattoo and he asked, "what do you want?" i said, "a circuit board on the side of my neck." he asked, "you know that is a job stopper?" i said, "i am going to be a programmer, they hire people with face tattoos." he laughed and asked, "why a circuit?" i said, "because my grandpa fixed machines and i fix code, and it is the same thing." it hurt like hell on the bone. raven held my hand and asked, "you okay?" i said, "i am going to bite you." she said, "later." when it was done i stared at it in the mirror and said, "now i look like what i am."

i had four dollars in my account and two weeks until payday. i asked raven, "how long can a person live on rice?" she asked, "do you need money?" i said, "no, i need rice." she said, "i can lend you fifty." i said, "i do not borrow money, that is how my mom drowned." she asked, "then can i buy us dinner and you buy next time?" i said, "that is borrowing with extra steps." she said, "it is dating, idiot." i laughed and let her buy the pizza. i paid her back the next week in quarters and she called me insane.

for my first college halloween raven and i went as the two ghost twins from the hotel movie. a guy at the party asked, "are you two sisters?" raven said, "come play with us." he backed away slowly. i laughed so hard i fell into the couch. a girl asked, "is this your first college halloween?" i said, "first one where nobody calls my mom." she asked, "what did you do in high school?" i said, "cemeteries, mostly." she said, "that is so dark." i said, "this party is dark too, the lights are off." raven said, "she means the ghost twins are proud."

raven asked, "why do you cry at every show?" i said, "because it is the only place where screaming is the right answer." she asked, "do you cry at church?" i said, "i have never been to church." she asked, "never?" i said, "my grandpa said the garage was his church and the pit was mine." she said, "then let us go to church." we went to a show in a basement and i screamed every word until my voice broke. after, she asked, "did you find god?" i said, "i found my throat is bleeding." she said, "same thing."

grandma pearl mailed me a box with a note that said, for college. inside was a black sweater she knitted and twenty dollars and a newspaper clipping about computers. i called her and asked, "did you knit this?" she said, "it took me a month, my fingers are old." i asked, "why black?" she said, "because you would not wear any other color, you stubborn thing." i said, "i love it." she asked, "are you warm?" i said, "i am now." she asked, "are you happy?" i said, "yes, grandma." she said, "good, then i can go to bingo."
